title: end-to-end-latency-profiling-traces-2026-03-20
content:
Context and goal:
We ran a focused end-to-end (E2E) latency profiling sweep across the hosted API stack to understand recent p95/p99 regressions observed in production (customer reports + synthetic checks). This doc contains: summary metrics, per-stage breakdowns from traces, hypothesis for root causes, quick experiments we ran, and next actions.

Test surface and configuration:
- Window: 2026-03-18 00:00 UTC through 2026-03-20 12:00 UTC (focused runs on 2026-03-20).
- Workloads: chat-completion typical (avg gen length 75 tokens), long completion (avg 350 tokens), streaming enabled vs disabled.
- Clients: synthetic runner in us-west1, 200 concurrent connections for 30s bursts, 1k requests per test.
- Model: rwd-open-13b-v2 (quantized int8 runtime profile), KV cache enabled for chat flows.
- Routing: hosted-main -> region gateway -> model pool (g4dn-like) -> runtime.
- Instrumentation: OpenTelemetry traces with stage spans: client->gateway, gateway->router, router->pool-assign, pool->worker (runtime), runtime:tokenize, kv-lookup, kv-apply, forward-attention, backward-kv, kernel-exec, post-process, response-serialize.

Summary metrics (p50 / p95 / p99) across all requests (chat typical):
- E2E (request start -> first byte of final response): p50=86ms, p95=420ms, p99=1.12s
- Gateway processing (ingress + auth + rate-limit): p50=12ms, p95=35ms, p99=110ms
- Router + pool-assign: p50=6ms, p95=18ms, p99=60ms
- Worker queue wait (time in pool queue when busy): p50=1ms, p95=120ms, p99=520ms
- Runtime total (worker start -> response serialize): p50=60ms, p95=240ms, p99=700ms
  - tokenize: p50=2ms, p95=6ms, p99=15ms
  - kv-lookup: p50=0.5ms, p95=3ms, p99=10ms
  - kv-apply (merge cached prefix): p50=1ms, p95=12ms, p99=45ms
  - kernel-exec (inference compute): p50=45ms, p95=180ms, p99=620ms
  - post-process (detokenize + safety checks): p50=3ms, p95=12ms, p99=30ms
  - response-serialize + net-send: p50=8ms, p95=20ms, p99=60ms

Observations and patterns:
1) High p95/p99 dominated by two contributors: worker queue wait and kernel-exec tail spikes.
   - Worker queue wait p95=120ms & p99=520ms indicates intermittent scheduling/backpressure events in dedicated pools. Correlates with CPU scheduling and short-lived worker GC spikes (see traces).
   - Kernel-exec p99=620ms is the largest single span inside runtime for heavy sequences: we see longer kernels when sequence length > 256 and when attention fusion path falls back to slower fallback kernel (observed on ~8% of requests).

2) KV cache applies introduce measurable variability at tail. kv-apply p99=45ms vs p95=12ms suggests lock contention occasionally when multiple in-flight requests target same chat session or same worker (cache synchronization).

3) Networking/gateway latency is small relative to runtime, but serialization/streaming shows extra variability when streaming is enabled and client buffers are small; TCP Nagle interactions observed on some runs — recommend keepalive/disable-nagle for streaming sockets.

Trace examples (representative):
- Trace A (p50 case): E2E=78ms: gateway 10ms / router 5ms / worker-queue 0ms / runtime 60ms (kernel-exec 44ms). Clean path: attention optimized kernel used, KV-cache hit short path.
- Trace B (p95 case): E2E=410ms: gateway 20ms / router 15ms / worker-queue 110ms / runtime 250ms (kernel-exec 160ms, kv-apply 12ms). Worker queue wait caused by transient burst; kernel path normal.
- Trace C (p99 case): E2E=1.15s: gateway 80ms (rare auth retry) / router 20ms / worker-queue 520ms / runtime 520ms (kernel-exec 430ms, kv-apply 45ms). Two contributors: pool saturation + fallback kernel + occasional remote KMS latency on safety checks (adds ~80ms).

Hypotheses (ranked):
- H1: Pool scheduling/backpressure + insufficient prewarming for bursty workloads -> high worker queue tail. Evidence: queue times spike during short 30s bursts; warm-pool size metric low before bursts.
- H2: Kernel selection logic sometimes chooses slower fallback kernels for certain position IDs and sequence alignments (alignment with our padded length heuristic). Evidence: kernel-exec traces show function name fallback_kernel_* on tails; ~8% of runs.
- H3: KV cache synchronization when multiple in-flight requests target same session leads to short locks. Evidence: kv-apply traces with lock-wait spans overlapping across concurrent traces to same worker.
- H4: Streaming TCP path suboptimal for small-chunk streaming due to Nagle/delayed ACK interactions.
- H5: Occasional external dependency latency (KMS for safety label checks) exacerbates tail for a small subset of requests.

Quick experiments & results (what we ran today):
- E1: Increased warm-pool target by 25% for 1h during synthetic bursts. Result: worker-queue p95 reduced from 120ms -> 45ms; p99 from 520ms -> 200ms. Cost impact: +8% GPU time.
- E2: Forced kernel path to preferred fused-attention kernel for eligible shapes (A/B test on 20% of traffic). Result: kernel-exec p95 reduced by ~30% for those flows; no correctness issues seen in sample outputs. We need longer validation for numerical parity.
- E3: Introduced optimistic read path for KV-apply (lock-free fast-path) in runtime branch rwd/kv-fast-path (dev). On small pilot load: kv-apply p99 dropped from 45ms -> 18ms for pilot.
- E4: Disabled Nagle for streaming sockets in client runner. Observed ~12-20ms improvement for first-chunk latency on small streams.

Recommended next actions (short-term):
- Roll out warm-pool increase as conservative default during business hours for hosted-main for next 2 weeks (owner: SRE; JIRA RINF-4321).
- Finish kernel selection A/B (expand to 50% traffic) and validate outputs across regen tests + eval suite (owner: eng-serving-runtime; PR #987).
- Merge KV fast-path after more unit tests and stress tests (owner: Priya Singh).
- Instrument additional trace attributes: pool-utilization, kernel-path-id, kv-lock-cause to improve diagnosis (owner: Miguel Rodriguez).
- Add alert: pool-queue-p99 > 300ms -> trigger autoscale burst and notify on-call.

Longer-term & research items:
- Investigate smarter pre-warm policies driven by traffic predictions (time-series).
- Revisit kernel compilation heuristics to reduce fallback occurrences (compiler team + runtime).
- Explore finer-grained per-session queue slots to avoid lock-step bursts for hot sessions.

Open questions / notes to self:
- Are there customers with very bursty single-session behavior we should surface to account teams? (ask CS).
- Need to validate KMS safety check path caching — can we cache labels per prompt fingerprint?
- Double-check whether quantization changes affect kernel selection distribution.

Appendix: quick command snippets used to run sweeps:
- synthetic runner: ./tools/latency_sweep --concurrency 200 --duration 30s --model rwd-open-13b-v2 --region us-west1 --streaming [on|off]
- query traces: otel-query "select span_name, p50(duration), p95(duration), p99(duration) by span_name where service=serving-runtime and time>\"2026-03-20\""

Links / artifacts:
- JIRA: RINF-4321 (warm pool autoscale and alerts)
- PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/987 (kernel-selection A/B)

Status: in_review — posting this for feedback from SRE and runtime compiler teams.

-- Emma
